prompt: Which best describes a design pattern?
explanation: A pattern is a general, reusable solution you adapt — not copy-paste code, not a library, and not an algorithm (which computes a result rather than arranging responsibilities).

options.text: A named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem that you adapt to your situation
A snippet of code you copy and paste unchanged
A library you install from npm
An algorithm like quicksort

prompt: Match each GoF category to what it is mainly about.
explanation: GoF sorts the 23 patterns into creational (how objects are made), structural (how they're assembled), and behavioral (how they interact).

prompt: Which statements about design patterns are TRUE? Select all that apply.
explanation: Patterns are a shared vocabulary, carry trade-offs, and are adaptable templates. Applying as many as possible is over-engineering — patterns are not a quality badge.

options.text: They give a team a shared vocabulary for design
They always make code better, so use as many as possible
They come with consequences and trade-offs
They describe an arrangement you adapt, not exact code

prompt: Complete the GoF principle: "Program to an ____, not an implementation."
explanation: Depending on an interface (what an object can do) rather than a concrete class (how it does it) lets you swap implementations freely.

prompt: Roughly how many patterns did the Gang of Four catalog, and in what year?
explanation: The 1994 GoF book cataloged 23 patterns. (Christopher Alexander's architectural book that inspired the idea was 1977.)

options.text: 23 patterns, in 1994
10 patterns, in 1977
50 patterns, in 2005
23 patterns, in 2015

prompt: A developer wraps a one-line config read in three interfaces, an Abstract Factory, and a Singleton 'to be enterprise-ready.' What is this an example of?
explanation: Patterns add classes and indirection. Applying them where simple code would do adds cost with no benefit — the definition of over-engineering.

options.text: Over-engineering — paying a pattern's cost with no matching benefit
Programming to an interface
Favoring composition over inheritance
A behavioral pattern

prompt: In a UML class diagram, which arrow style represents an implementation/realization relationship from a class to an interface?

options.text: A dashed line with an open, hollow triangle pointing to the interface
A solid line with a solid diamond
A dashed line with a simple open arrowhead
A solid bold line with no arrowheads

explanation: In UML, a dashed line with a hollow triangle represents realization/implementation of an interface. A solid line with a hollow triangle represents class inheritance/generalization.

prompt: Why does the Gang of Four advocate "Favor object composition over class inheritance"?

options.text: Composition allows behaviors to be swapped dynamically at runtime and avoids rigid compile-time coupling
Inheritance is deprecated and forbidden in modern TypeScript
Composition uses less memory than inheritance hierarchies
Inheritance prevents subclasses from accessing public methods

explanation: Inheritance binds behavior at compile time and breaks encapsulation (white-box reuse). Composition delegates to injected interfaces, enabling runtime swapping (black-box reuse).

prompt: Which of the following conditions indicate that introducing a design pattern is justified? Select all that apply.

options.text: A concrete code smell or variation point has emerged in production code
You want your application architecture to look more enterprise-ready before writing business logic
Requirements demand swapping algorithmic implementations or data sources dynamically
Multiple classes share duplicate structural wiring or recursive hierarchies

explanation: Patterns should solve concrete pressures: dynamic swapping, recursive hierarchies, or real code smells. Applying patterns speculatively before requirements exist is over-engineering.

prompt: In UML notation, what is the key difference between Aggregation and Composition?

options.text: Composition (solid diamond) implies strict ownership where child parts cannot exist without the parent container; Aggregation (hollow diamond) implies a weaker whole-part association where parts outlive the container
Aggregation implies strict ownership, while Composition is temporary
Aggregation only applies to interfaces; Composition only applies to abstract classes
Composition is drawn with a dashed arrow; Aggregation is drawn with a solid line

explanation: Composition is strong ownership (death of parent deletes children, represented by a filled diamond). Aggregation is weak ownership (parts exist independently, represented by an unfilled hollow diamond).

prompt: Match each SOLID letter to its principle.
explanation: SOLID stands for Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion.

prompt: The Open/Closed Principle says software entities should be:
explanation: OCP means you add new behavior by adding new code, without editing existing, already-tested code.

options.text: Open for extension but closed for modification
Open source but closed to outside contributors
Closed for extension but open for modification
Always rewritten when requirements change

prompt: A Penguin class extends Bird but overrides fly() to throw an error. Which principle does this most clearly violate?
explanation: A Penguin can't stand in for a Bird wherever fly() is called, so it breaks substitutability — an LSP violation the compiler won't catch.

options.text: Liskov Substitution Principle
Single Responsibility Principle
Interface Segregation Principle
Open/Closed Principle

prompt: The 'D' in SOLID is the Dependency ____ Principle: depend on abstractions, not concretions.
explanation: Dependency Inversion: high-level code and low-level details both depend on an abstraction in the middle.

prompt: Which statements about Dependency Inversion (DIP), Dependency Injection (DI), and Inversion of Control (IoC) are TRUE? Select all that apply.
explanation: DIP is the principle, DI is a technique that achieves it, and IoC is the broader idea — they are related but distinct. DI is not one of the 23 GoF patterns.

options.text: DIP is a principle: depend on abstractions
DI is a technique: pass dependencies in instead of creating them internally
DI, DIP, and IoC are three names for exactly the same thing
DI is a Gang of Four design pattern

prompt: Splitting a fat AllInOne { print, scan, fax } interface into separate Printer and Scanner interfaces follows which principle?
explanation: ISP says prefer small, client-specific interfaces so a class isn't forced to implement methods (like fax) it doesn't use.

options.text: Interface Segregation Principle
Liskov Substitution Principle
Single Responsibility Principle
Dependency Inversion Principle

prompt: According to Robert C. Martin, what is the precise definition of 'responsibility' in the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?

options.text: A class should have one, and only one, reason to change (meaning it is accountable to only one actor or stakeholder)
A class must have only one public method
A class must not import more than one external module
A class should perform only one mathematical operation per turn

explanation: SRP defines a responsibility as a reason to change, anchored to the business actor or stakeholder who requests that change (e.g., accounting vs. human resources).

prompt: How does an Inversion of Control (IoC) container differ from direct Dependency Injection (DI)?

options.text: An IoC container automates the lifecycle, instantiation, and resolution of dependencies across an application graph
IoC containers eliminate the need for interfaces
DI requires an IoC container, while DIP does not
IoC containers execute code synchronously without inversion

explanation: Dependency Injection is the technique of passing dependencies into a constructor or method. An IoC container is an automated framework mechanism that manages instantiation, scoping, and resolution across the object graph.

prompt: Which of the following violate the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)? Select all that apply.

options.text: A subclass strengthens preconditions, requiring stricter parameters than the base interface
A subclass weakens postconditions, failing to guarantee state conditions established by the base class
A subclass overrides a method to throw an unsupported operation error
A subclass returns a more specific subtype (covariant return type) of the interface return type

explanation: LSP requires that subtypes must not strengthen preconditions, must not weaken postconditions, and must not throw unexpected exceptions for valid base-type inputs. Covariant return types are permitted and safe.

prompt: How do Strategy and Decorator design patterns help fulfill the Open/Closed Principle (OCP)?

options.text: They allow new algorithms or behaviors to be introduced by adding new classes without editing existing client or core logic
They convert private fields into public fields
They merge multiple interfaces into a single omnibus interface
They eliminate polymorphism in favor of switch statements

explanation: Strategy and Decorator keep existing classes closed to modification while keeping the system open for extension by injecting new polymorphic strategy or decorator classes.

prompt: What is the intent of the Factory Method pattern?
explanation: Factory Method defers instantiation of a single product to subclasses. (One instance = Singleton; families = Abstract Factory; runtime responsibilities = Decorator.)

options.text: Define a method for creating an object but let subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate
Ensure a class has only one instance
Create whole families of related objects at once
Add responsibilities to an object at runtime

prompt: Which mechanism does Factory Method use to vary which product is created?
explanation: A concrete creator subclass overrides the factory method to return its product. (Composition is how Abstract Factory varies products; cloning is Prototype.)

options.text: Inheritance — a subclass overrides the factory method
Composition — you hold a separate factory object
Reflection over class names
Cloning an existing instance

prompt: In Factory Method, the higher-level code should depend on the Product ____ rather than a concrete product class.
explanation: Returning and using the Product interface keeps the creator decoupled from concrete products.

prompt: Which are genuine benefits of Factory Method? Select all that apply.
explanation: Factory Method decouples use from creation, supports OCP, and centralizes creation. Guaranteeing a single instance is Singleton, not Factory Method.

options.text: It decouples the code that uses a product from the code that creates it
Adding a new product can be done by adding a subclass, without editing existing code (OCP)
It guarantees only one product instance ever exists
It centralizes creation logic in one method

prompt: In TypeScript, what is a common lighter-weight alternative to a Factory Method subclass?
explanation: Because functions are first-class in TS, a factory function can carry the creation decision without defining a new subclass.

options.text: Passing a factory function that returns the product
Using a global variable
Deep-cloning the creator
Making every field public

prompt: What is the main downside of Factory Method?
explanation: You may create a whole subclass to vary one product, which is overkill when a parameter or factory function would do.

options.text: It can multiply subclasses, sometimes just to change one product
It makes objects impossible to test
It requires a database
It always slows programs down

prompt: What is the intent of the Abstract Factory pattern?
explanation: Abstract Factory is about families of related products. Single product via subclass = Factory Method; step-by-step = Builder; one instance = Singleton.

options.text: Provide an interface for creating families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes
Let subclasses decide which single class to instantiate
Build a complex object step by step
Restrict a class to a single instance

prompt: The KEY difference between Abstract Factory and Factory Method is:
explanation: Abstract Factory = family + composition (hold a factory object); Factory Method = one product + inheritance (override a method).

options.text: Abstract Factory creates a family of products via composition; Factory Method creates one product via inheritance
They are two names for the same pattern
Abstract Factory uses inheritance; Factory Method uses composition
Abstract Factory can only create one product

prompt: Abstract Factory produces a matched ____ of related products that are meant to be used together.
explanation: The point is a consistent family/set — e.g. all-light or all-dark widgets — so incompatible products can't be mixed.

prompt: What is the main weakness of Abstract Factory?
explanation: The set of product kinds is baked into the factory interface, so introducing a new kind ripples through all factories.

options.text: Adding a new KIND of product forces changes to the factory interface and every concrete factory
It cannot guarantee product consistency
It makes objects impossible to swap
It only works with a database

prompt: Match each concrete factory to the products it should create.
explanation: Each concrete factory produces exactly one internally consistent family, so pieces always match.

prompt: When is Abstract Factory a good fit? Select all that apply.
explanation: Abstract Factory shines when families vary but the set of product kinds is stable. Frequently adding new product kinds is exactly where it becomes rigid.

options.text: Products must be used together and mixing them would be a bug
You want to swap an entire set of products at once
You frequently add brand-new kinds of product to the set
The set of product kinds is stable, but the families vary

prompt: What is the intent of the Builder pattern?
explanation: Builder is about constructing a complex object in steps. One instance = Singleton; cloning = Prototype; converting interfaces = Adapter.

options.text: Separate the step-by-step construction of a complex object from its final representation
Guarantee a class has only one instance
Create a new object by cloning an existing one
Convert one interface into another

prompt: Builder replaces the ____ constructor smell — long, overloaded constructors with many positional parameters.
explanation: The telescoping constructor (growing overloaded parameter lists) is exactly what Builder is meant to remove.

prompt: In a fluent builder, why does each step method return `this`?
explanation: Returning `this` lets you write builder.withA().withB().build() as one readable chain.

options.text: So the calls can be chained together
To make the object a singleton
To deep-copy the object
To hide the constructor

prompt: How does Builder differ from a Factory?
explanation: The distinguishing feature is step-by-step construction (builder) versus a single creation call (factory).

options.text: A factory returns an object in one call; a builder assembles it over several named steps
They are identical
A builder can only make one instance ever
A factory always uses inheritance and a builder never does

prompt: What is the optional Director's job in the GoF Builder?
explanation: A Director encapsulates a construction recipe so it can be reused; it's optional and often omitted.

options.text: It runs a fixed sequence of builder steps (a reusable recipe)
It stores the single global instance
It converts the product to another interface
It notifies observers when the product changes

prompt: When is Builder the WRONG choice?
explanation: For simple objects a constructor or literal is clearer; Builder's ceremony only pays off for complex construction.

options.text: For a simple object with only a couple of fields
For an object with many optional parts
When you want validation centralized in build()
When you want an immutable result

prompt: What is the intent of the Prototype pattern?
explanation: Prototype creates objects by cloning. One instance = Singleton; step-by-step = Builder; simplified interface = Facade.

options.text: Create new objects by copying an existing prototypical instance
Ensure only one instance of a class exists
Build a complex object step by step
Provide a simplified interface to a subsystem

prompt: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
explanation: Shallow duplicates only the top level (nested objects are shared); deep duplicates all levels.

options.text: A shallow copy shares nested objects; a deep copy duplicates every level so nothing is shared
A shallow copy is always slower than a deep copy
A deep copy shares nested objects; a shallow copy duplicates everything
They are the same thing

prompt: Why is a clone() that does `Object.assign(new Thing(), this)` often a bug?
explanation: Top-level assignment leaves nested references shared, so mutating one 'copy' changes the other.

options.text: It is a shallow copy, so the clone shares the original's nested objects and arrays
It always throws an exception
It creates two singletons
It permanently freezes the original

prompt: Which statements about structuredClone() are TRUE? Select all that apply.
explanation: structuredClone deep-copies data but drops methods/prototype (returns a plain object) and can't clone functions.

options.text: It performs a deep copy of plain data
It preserves a class instance's methods and prototype
It cannot clone functions
It returns a plain object when given a class instance

prompt: How does the Prototype pattern relate to JavaScript's prototypal inheritance?
explanation: The Prototype pattern is about cloning; JS prototypal inheritance is a language feature for sharing methods. Same word, different concept.

options.text: They share a name but are different ideas: the pattern copies objects, prototypal inheritance shares behavior via a linked prototype
They are exactly the same mechanism
Prototypal inheritance is a way to guarantee a single instance
The pattern only works in languages without prototypes

prompt: When is Prototype especially useful?
explanation: Cloning a prepared prototype is cheaper than rebuilding, and avoids a factory subclass per configuration.

options.text: When constructing an object from scratch is expensive and you need many similar copies
When you must forbid copying entirely
When an object should have exactly one instance
When two incompatible interfaces must work together

prompt: What is the intent of the Singleton pattern?
explanation: Singleton restricts a class to one instance with global access. Cloning = Prototype; step-by-step = Builder; families = Abstract Factory.

options.text: Ensure a class has only one instance and provide a global point of access to it
Create objects by cloning a prototype
Build a complex object step by step
Create families of related products

prompt: Which are common, valid criticisms of Singleton? Select all that apply.
explanation: Singleton's downsides are global state, hidden dependencies, and testing pain. It has nothing to do with speed.

options.text: It introduces global mutable state
It hides a class's real dependencies
It makes unit testing harder because state leaks between tests
It always makes programs run faster

prompt: Which two things make a class a Singleton? Select all that apply.
explanation: A private constructor blocks outside instantiation; a static accessor lazily creates and returns the one instance.

options.text: A private constructor
A static accessor that returns the single instance
A clone() method
A fluent build() method

prompt: Why is a Singleton class often unnecessary in TypeScript?
explanation: Modules run once and their exports are shared across imports, giving a single instance without the Singleton ceremony.

options.text: An ES module is evaluated once, so a module-level export is already a single shared instance
TypeScript forbids the `new` keyword
TypeScript objects are automatically global
Classes cannot have static members in TypeScript

prompt: Is the classic 'two threads create two instances' thread-safety concern relevant in JavaScript?
explanation: Single-threaded JS avoids that race; the synchronization concern applies to languages like Java, C#, and C++.

options.text: No — JavaScript is single-threaded, so that race doesn't occur (it matters in multi-threaded languages)
Yes — JavaScript runs every function on its own thread
Yes — and it can only be fixed with locks in JavaScript
It is impossible to create a Singleton in JavaScript

prompt: For most application code, what is usually a better alternative to fetching a Singleton?
explanation: Injecting a single instance keeps dependencies visible and lets tests substitute a fake — avoiding Singleton's worst problems.

options.text: Dependency Injection — create one instance and pass it in, keeping dependencies explicit
Copying the object with a shallow clone everywhere
Making every field public and global
Adding more static methods

prompt: What is the intent of the Adapter pattern?
explanation: Adapter changes one interface into a different expected one. Adding behavior = Decorator; simplifying a subsystem = Facade; controlling access = Proxy.

options.text: Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect
Add new behavior to an object while keeping its interface
Provide a simplified interface to a complex subsystem
Control access to another object

prompt: Match each Adapter participant to its role.
explanation: The adapter implements the Target and forwards calls to the Adaptee, so the Client only sees the Target.

pairs.right: The interface the client wants to use
The existing class with an incompatible interface
Implements the target and delegates to the adaptee

prompt: Why do TypeScript adapters typically use composition (an 'object adapter')?
explanation: Class adapters need multiple inheritance; TypeScript classes have single inheritance, so the adapter composes (holds) the adaptee.

options.text: The adapter holds the adaptee, which suits TypeScript's single-inheritance classes
TypeScript forbids interfaces
Because composition is always slower
Because TypeScript supports multiple inheritance of classes

prompt: Adapter is most useful at integration ____ — third-party libraries or legacy modules whose interface you can't change.
explanation: Adapters belong at boundaries you don't own or shouldn't modify, centralizing the translation there.

prompt: How does Adapter differ from Facade?
explanation: Adapter is about interface conversion; Facade is about presenting a simpler front to many classes.

options.text: Adapter makes one interface look like a different expected interface; Facade simplifies a complex subsystem
They are the same pattern
Adapter adds behavior; Facade removes behavior
Adapter controls access; Facade clones objects

prompt: Which is a sign you might be MISUSING Adapter?
explanation: Adapters are for boundaries you can't change; adapting code you own can just paper over an inconsistent design you should fix.

options.text: Using it to hide a mismatch between two interfaces you own and could align directly
Using it to wrap a third-party library you can't modify
Keeping the adapter thin and free of business logic
Letting the client depend only on the Target interface

prompt: What is the intent of the Bridge pattern?
explanation: Bridge separates two dimensions so each can change independently. Converting interfaces = Adapter; trees = Composite; one instance = Singleton.

options.text: Decouple an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently
Convert one interface into another
Compose objects into tree structures
Ensure a class has one instance

prompt: What problem does Bridge primarily prevent?
explanation: Combining N shapes with M renderers via inheritance needs N×M subclasses; Bridge makes it N+M across two hierarchies.

options.text: The combinatorial explosion of subclasses from combining two dimensions via inheritance
Two threads creating two instances
Shallow copies sharing state
Fat interfaces forcing unused methods

prompt: What is the 'bridge' between the two hierarchies?
explanation: The abstraction composes an implementor interface and delegates low-level work to it — that link is the bridge.

options.text: A composition link: the abstraction holds and delegates to an implementation interface
A shared base class both inherit from
A global singleton registry
A clone() method

prompt: How does Bridge differ from Adapter?
explanation: Bridge is a planned separation; Adapter is a reactive fix for a mismatch you didn't plan for.

options.text: Bridge is designed up front to keep two dimensions independent; Adapter reconciles two existing incompatible interfaces after the fact
They are identical
Bridge only works with third-party code
Adapter always creates families of objects

prompt: When is Bridge overkill?
explanation: With only one implementation there's no second axis to decouple, so the extra interface and delegation add no value.

options.text: When there is really only one dimension of change (e.g. a single implementation)
When both the abstraction and implementation grow over time
When you want to swap implementations at runtime
When you have many shapes and many renderers

prompt: Which are genuine benefits of Bridge? Select all that apply.
explanation: Bridge gives independent evolution, runtime switching, and linear (not multiplicative) growth. Single-instance guarantees are Singleton's job.

options.text: Abstraction and implementation can evolve independently
You can switch the implementation at runtime
It guarantees a single global instance
New variants on either side are added without multiplying subclasses

prompt: What is the intent of the Composite pattern?
explanation: Composite is about part-whole trees with uniform treatment. Decoupling two dimensions = Bridge; adding responsibilities = Decorator; one instance = Singleton.

options.text: Compose objects into tree structures and let clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly
Decouple an abstraction from its implementation
Attach responsibilities to an object dynamically
Ensure a single instance

prompt: Match each Composite role to its description.
explanation: Leaves and composites share the Component interface; composites implement operations by delegating to their children.

pairs.right: The shared interface for all nodes
A node that holds children and delegates to them

prompt: How does a composite typically implement an operation such as size()?
explanation: A folder's size() sums the sizes of its children, each of which may itself be a folder — recursion through the tree.

options.text: By recursing — delegating to each child and combining the results
By cloning itself
By converting its interface to another
By storing a single global value

prompt: Composite represents ____-whole hierarchies, where wholes are made of parts that may themselves be wholes.
explanation: The pattern models part-whole hierarchies such as files within folders within folders.

prompt: What is the well-known design tension in Composite?
explanation: Putting child-management on the Component forces leaves to implement methods that don't apply, often by throwing — a Liskov trade-off.

options.text: Whether add/remove belong on the shared Component (forcing leaves to implement them) or only on the Composite
Whether to use a private constructor
Whether to deep-copy or shallow-copy
Whether to inject dependencies

prompt: When is Composite the WRONG choice?
explanation: Composite earns its keep only with real nesting; a flat list gains nothing from it.

options.text: When the data is a flat collection, not a genuine tree
When you have folders nested inside folders
When you want to treat leaves and groups uniformly
When a UI panel contains other panels

prompt: What is the intent of the Decorator pattern?
explanation: Decorator adds behavior dynamically while keeping the same interface. Converting interfaces = Adapter; trees = Composite; simplifying = Facade.

options.text: Attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically, as a flexible alternative to subclassing
Convert one interface into another
Compose objects into tree structures
Provide a simplified interface to a subsystem

prompt: What does a decorator keep the same as the object it wraps?
explanation: A decorator implements the same Component interface, so it's transparent to callers and can be stacked.

options.text: Its interface, so clients can't tell it's wrapped
Its exact memory address
Nothing — it changes the interface
Its private constructor

prompt: How does Decorator differ from Proxy?
explanation: Decorator and Proxy both wrap with the same interface; the difference is intent — adding responsibilities vs controlling access.

options.text: Both keep the same interface, but Decorator adds behavior while Proxy controls access
Decorator changes the interface; Proxy keeps it
They are the same pattern
Proxy adds behavior; Decorator clones the object

prompt: What common bug breaks a decorator chain?
explanation: Decorators must delegate calls they don't specifically change; forgetting to forward makes the wrapped behavior vanish.

options.text: Overriding a method but forgetting to forward the call to the wrapped object
Using an interface
Making the base component immutable
Injecting the component

prompt: How is the GoF Decorator pattern different from TypeScript's @decorator language feature?
explanation: Same name, different mechanism: one is a runtime object-wrapping pattern, the other is annotation syntax.

options.text: The GoF Decorator is a wrapping design pattern; @decorator is a language feature for annotating classes/members
They are identical
The GoF Decorator only works with the @ syntax
@decorator can only create singletons

prompt: Which are advantages of Decorator over subclassing every combination? Select all that apply.
explanation: Decorator gives runtime combination, avoids the combinatorial subclass explosion, and keeps each wrapper focused. Single-instance is Singleton.

options.text: Behaviors can be combined at runtime in any order
It avoids a class explosion of feature combinations
Each decorator can stay small and single-purpose
It guarantees only one instance of the object

prompt: What is the intent of the Facade pattern?
explanation: Facade simplifies a subsystem behind one interface. Converting an interface = Adapter; adding responsibilities = Decorator; cloning = Prototype.

options.text: Provide a unified, higher-level interface that makes a complex subsystem easier to use
Convert one class's interface into another
Add responsibilities to an object dynamically
Clone objects from a prototype

prompt: Does a Facade prevent callers from using the subsystem directly?
explanation: A facade simplifies the common case without hiding or forbidding direct subsystem access for edge cases.

options.text: No — it offers an easy path but leaves the subsystem reachable for advanced needs
Yes — the subsystem becomes completely inaccessible
Yes — it deletes the subsystem classes
Only if the subsystem is a singleton

prompt: How does Facade differ from Adapter?
explanation: Facade = simplify many; Adapter = convert one interface into a specific expected interface.

options.text: Facade wraps many classes behind a new simpler interface; Adapter converts one object's interface to a specific expected one
They are identical
Facade changes an interface; Adapter simplifies a subsystem
Facade controls access; Adapter adds behavior

prompt: What is the main risk of a Facade over time?
explanation: If every feature is bolted on, the facade relocates the complexity it was meant to hide — the god-object anti-pattern.

options.text: It can swell into a god object that accumulates too many responsibilities
It forces two threads to collide
It always makes the subsystem slower
It prevents dependency injection

prompt: A key benefit of Facade is that it reduces ____ between client code and a complex subsystem.
explanation: Clients depend on the single facade instead of many subsystem internals, lowering coupling.

prompt: In the order example, what does placeOrder() encode so clients don't have to?
explanation: The facade captures the workflow and ordering across subsystems so each caller doesn't repeat it.

options.text: The correct sequence: reserve inventory, then charge payment, then schedule shipping
The single global instance of the order
How to deep-copy the order
How to convert the order to another interface

prompt: What is the intent of the Flyweight pattern?
explanation: Flyweight shares common state to save memory across many objects. Simplifying = Facade; one instance = Singleton; converting = Adapter.

options.text: Use sharing to support large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently
Provide a simplified interface to a subsystem
Ensure a class has one instance
Convert one interface into another

prompt: Match each kind of state to its description.
explanation: Intrinsic state is shared and immutable; extrinsic state (like coordinates) is unique per object and supplied from outside.

pairs.right: Shared, context-independent, stored in the flyweight
Unique per use, kept outside and passed in

prompt: Why must a flyweight's intrinsic state be immutable?
explanation: Shared state that could change would affect every object referencing the flyweight, so it must be immutable.

options.text: Because it is shared across many objects, so a change would corrupt all of them
Because TypeScript forbids mutation
Because it makes the objects singletons
Because extrinsic state can't exist otherwise

prompt: What does the flyweight factory guarantee?
explanation: The factory caches and returns shared instances, creating one only when a genuinely new intrinsic combination appears.

options.text: That flyweights are reused — a new one is created only for a new combination of intrinsic state
That every request returns a brand-new object
That objects are deep-copied
That the subsystem is hidden

prompt: Flyweight's explicit goal is to save ____ when there are very many similar objects.
explanation: It is the one GoF pattern whose stated purpose is efficient memory use across large numbers of objects.

prompt: When is Flyweight the WRONG choice?
explanation: Flyweight only pays off at large scale with shared data; with few objects or all-unique state it just adds complexity.

options.text: When you have only a modest number of objects, or each object's data is unique
When you have millions of objects sharing common data
When memory is the bottleneck
When many objects share the same texture

prompt: What is the intent of the Proxy pattern?
explanation: Proxy controls access via a same-interface stand-in. Adding responsibilities = Decorator; converting = Adapter; sharing state = Flyweight.

options.text: Provide a surrogate with the same interface that controls access to another object
Add responsibilities to an object dynamically
Convert one interface into another
Share intrinsic state across many objects

prompt: Match each proxy variety to what it does.
explanation: Proxies are categorized by purpose: lazy loading, access control, remoting, and caching.

pairs.right: Defers creating an expensive object until needed
Represents an object in another process/machine
Stores results to avoid repeat work

prompt: Both Proxy and Decorator keep the same interface as the wrapped object. What distinguishes them?
explanation: The tell is intent: Decorator enriches behavior, Proxy gatekeeps access (lazy, secure, cached, remote).

options.text: Decorator adds responsibilities; Proxy controls access
Decorator changes the interface; Proxy does not
Proxy adds responsibilities; Decorator controls access
They are the same pattern

prompt: Match each wrapper pattern to how its interface relates to the wrapped object.
explanation: Adapter converts, Facade simplifies many, Decorator adds behavior (same interface), Proxy controls access (same interface).

pairs.right: A new, simpler interface over many classes
The same interface, with added behavior
